Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 1:

﴿Who made the angels messengers﴾ meaning intermediaries between Allah and the prophets, who carry out the affairs of Allah. ﴿Having wings, two, three, or four﴾ These are descriptions of the wings. It is not declined (ghayr munsarif) because of the two reasons of ʿadl (equivalence to another form) and wasf (adjectival form). The meaning is that among the angels, some have two wings, some have three wings, and some have four wings. ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ It has been said: this means a beautiful voice; and it has been said: a beautiful face; and it has been said: good fortune. The most apparent view is that it refers to the wings of the angels, or that it is general, covering every increase in created beings.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 2:

﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release it after Him.﴾

Al-fath (opening, i.e. bestowing) is an expression for giving, and al-imsak (withholding) is an expression for preventing. Al-irsal (release) is unrestricted granting after prevention. Al-rahmah (mercy) is everything that Allah bestows upon His servants of the good of this world and the Hereafter. So the meaning of the verse is: there is no preventer of what Allah has given, and no giver of what Allah has withheld.

If it is asked: why did he make the pronoun feminine in His saying ﴿فَلاَ مُمْسِكَ لَهَا﴾ ("none can withhold it") and masculine in His saying ﴿فَلاَ مُرْسِلَ لَهُ﴾ ("none can release it"), when both refer back to the conditional ما (mā)? The answer: when he explained the first ﴿مِن﴾ (min, "whatever") by His saying ﴿مِن رَّحْمَةٍ﴾ (mercy), he made the pronoun feminine to agree with the feminine noun rahmah, and he left the other on its original masculine form. ﴿مِن بَعْدِهِ﴾ (min ba'dihi, "after Him"), i.e., after His withholding it.

"Is there any creator other than Allah" (Hal min khaliqin ghayru Allah). Ghayr is read in the nominative as an adjective (sifah) of khaliq, taking the place (mahall) of the noun, and in the genitive as an adjective of the noun in its apparent form (raf', i.e., the nominative of the word itself). The provision of the sky is the rain, and the provision of the earth is the plants. The meaning is a reminder of Allah's favours and an establishment of proof against the polytheists. For this reason he follows it with His saying: "There is no god but He" (La ilaha illa Huwa).

Translation:

﴿And if they deny you﴾, [this verse is] a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ regarding his people's denial, as if it said: "If they deny you, do not grieve over that, for Allah will surely grant you victory over them, just as messengers before you were denied and Allah granted them victory."

Translation of the passage:

﴿al-gharur﴾ (the Deceiver): al-Shaytan (Satan). It is also said: it is procrastination (al-taswif).

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 35, verse 8:

﴿Is he, to whom the evil of his deeds has been made to look good, [equal to one who sees it as good]?﴾ This is a rhetorical question (tawqif, a question that demands the listener's acknowledgment), and its answer is omitted. The intended meaning is: "Is he to whom the evil of his deeds has been made to look good like one to whom it has not been made to look good?" He then built what follows on this. So the one to whom the evil of his deeds has been made to look good is the one whom Allah has misguided, and the one to whom the evil of his deeds has not been made to look good is the one whom Allah has guided. ﴿So let not your soul waste away in grief over them﴾. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding his sorrow over their lack of faith, because that is in the hand of Allah.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on surah 35, verse 9:

﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾. That is, the gathering (al-hashr) on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: just as Allah brings the earth to life with vegetation, so too He brings the dead to life.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 35, verse 10:**

﴿Whoever desires honour—then to Allah belongs all honour.﴾ The verse may carry three meanings. The first, and the most apparent, is: whoever wishes to attain honour should seek it from Allah, for all honour belongs to Allah. The second: whoever wishes to gain honour by opposing Islam, then to Allah belongs all honour, so whoever opposes Him is overcome. The third: whoever wishes to know to whom honour belongs, let him know that all honour belongs to Allah.

﴿To Him ascend the good words.﴾ It has been said that this means "there is no god but Allah." The wording, however, includes that and other forms of remembrance, supplication, recitation of the Qur'an, and teaching of knowledge. The general meaning is preferable.

﴿And righteous deeds He raises.﴾ On this there are three opinions. The first is that the pronoun of the subject in *yarfa'uhu* (He raises it) refers to Allah, and the pronoun of the object refers to the righteous deed. The meaning on this view is that Allah raises the righteous deed, that is, He accepts it and rewards it. The second is that the pronoun of the subject refers to the good words, and the pronoun of the object refers to the righteous deed. The meaning on this view is: no righteous deed is accepted except from one who has good words. This holds if we say that the good word is "there is no god but Allah," since deeds are accepted only from one who professes the Oneness of Allah. The third is that the pronoun of the subject refers to the righteous deed, and the pronoun of the object refers to the good words. The meaning on this view is that it is the righteous deed that raises the good words, so no words are accepted except from one who has a righteous deed. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but Ibn 'Atiyya considered it unlikely and said: "It is not authentically reported from him, because the belief of the People of the Sunnah (ahl al-sunnah, the adherents of the prophetic tradition and the consensus of the early community) is that Allah accepts from every Muslim." He said: "It may be sound if it is interpreted as meaning that Allah increases its elevation and the excellence of its standing."

﴿Those who plot evil deeds.﴾ The verb *yamkurun* (they plot) does not take a direct object, so its interpretation is: "they plot the evil plots." Thus *al-sayyi'at* (the evil deeds) is either a verbal noun (masdar) or the verb is understood to carry the sense of "they earn," in which case *al-sayyi'at* is the object. The reference here is to the plotting of the Quraysh against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they gathered in the House of Assembly (Dar al-Nadwa) and intended to kill him, imprison him, or expel him.

﴿And the plotting of those—it will come to ruin.﴾ *Al-bawar* means destruction or stagnation. Its meaning here is that their plotting will be nullified and will not benefit them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 11:

﴿Then He made you pairs﴾ i.e., kinds (aṣnāf). It was also said: males and females, and this is more apparent. ﴿And no one is granted a long life, nor is any part of his life shortened, except that it is in a Book﴾ al-ta'mīr (granting long life) is the lengthening of life; al-naqṣ (shortening) is its shortening; and al-Kitāb (the Book) is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). If it is said: granting long life and shortening cannot both apply to one and the same person, so how does the pronoun return in His words ﴿nor is any part of his life shortened﴾ to the person granted long life? The answer is in three aspects. The first, which is the correct one, is that the meaning is: no one [of mankind] is granted long life, nor is any part of the life of anyone shortened, except that it is in a Book. So "min mu'ammar" (of one who is granted long life) is placed in the position of "min aḥad" (of anyone), and the intended meaning is not one specific individual. This is like your saying: "God does not punish a servant, nor reward him, except with justice." The second: the meaning is that no increase is made in the life of a human being, nor is any part of his life decreased, except that it is in a Book; that is, it is written in the Preserved Tablet that so-and-so, if he gives charity, his life will be sixty years, and if he does not give charity, his life will be forty. This is the apparent meaning of the statement of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Maintaining family ties increases one's lifespan." However, this is the view of the Mu'tazila, who hold the doctrine of two terms (al-ajalayn), and it is not the view of the Ash'arites. Ka'b said when ʿUmar was stabbed: "If he had asked God, He would have added to his term." People disapproved of him, so he argued with this verse. The third: al-ta'mīr is the writing of the life that is yet to come, and al-naqṣ is the writing of what has passed of it in the Preserved Tablet, and that is the due of every person.

﴿Nor are the two seas alike﴾. We have already explained the two seas, the sweet (al-Furat) and the salty (al-Ajaj), in Surat al-Furqan [53], and the word "sweet" (sa'igh) in Surat al-Nahl [66]. The purpose of the verse is to draw attention to God's power, His oneness, and His favour upon His servants. Al-Zamakhshari said that the meaning is that God struck, for the two seas, the salty and the sweet, as parables for the believer and the disbeliever, but this is far-fetched. ﴿Fresh flesh﴾ means the fish. ﴿Ornaments you wear﴾ means the jewels and the coral. If it is said: ornaments come only out of the salty sea and not the sweet, so how does He say ﴿and from each﴾, that is, from each one of the two? The answer has three aspects. The first is that this is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) in expression, as in His words: ﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [al-An'am: 130], while the messengers were only from mankind. The second is that coral is found only in the salty sea, where rivers of sweet water pour out and where rain falls; since the rivers and the rain, which are sweet water, pour into the salty sea, the extraction is from both together. The third is that some people claimed that pearls and coral are extracted from both the salty and the sweet, but this view is refuted by the senses, that is, by observed reality. ﴿Ploughing﴾ (mawakhir): the word was explained in Surat al-Nahl [14], where it means ships cutting through the water.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 13:

﴿يُولِجُ﴾ (He causes to enter) was mentioned in Luqman [29]. ﴿قِطْمِيرٍ﴾ (qitmir) is the thin white membrane that lies over the date pit. The meaning is that the idols do not possess even the smallest of things, so how could they possess most of them?

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 14:

﴿They will disown your association (of partners with Allah)﴾ meaning, their disowning of your associating (others with Him). The verbal noun is thus annexed to its agent. The disowning of the idols of the association may be by a speech that Allah creates in them, or by the indication of the situation. ﴿And none can inform you like one who is All-Aware﴾ meaning, no informant informs you of the matter like one who has knowledge of it, namely Allah Himself, in His informing that the idols will disown, on the Day of Resurrection, those who worshipped them.

"You are the poor toward God," is addressed to all people. The definite article in "al-fuqara'" (the poor) is used to show that poverty is specific to the human race; although other beings are also poor, the poverty of humankind is greater. Then He described Himself as "the Rich" (al-Ghani) in contrast to their description as poor, and described Himself as "the Praiseworthy" (al-Hamid) to indicate His existence and His generosity, which necessitates that His servants praise Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 18:

﴿And if a heavily burdened soul calls out for someone to carry its load, nothing of it will be carried.﴾ Al-haml (the load) refers to sins. Muthqalah means one who is heavy with its load, or a soul burdened with many sins. The meaning is that even if it calls someone to bear its sins for it, nothing will be borne on its behalf. The object of ﴿tad'u﴾ (calls) is omitted because the meaning indicates it and because generality is intended. This verse explains and completes the meaning of His saying: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. ﴿Even if he were a close relative﴾: the meaning is that even if the one called upon is a close relative of the one who calls him to bear his sins, he will not bear any of them, because each person will say: "myself, myself." ﴿You can only warn those who fear their Lord﴾: the meaning is that warning benefits only those who fear their Lord, and it does not mean that warning is restricted to them. ﴿Unseen﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿yakhshawna﴾ (they fear), meaning they fear their Lord while they are absent from people, so their fear is genuine and not ostentatious.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verses 19–21:

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ is an illustration of the disbeliever and the believer. ﴿Nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ is an illustration of disbelief and faith. ﴿Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ is an illustration of reward and punishment. It is also said: ﴿the shade﴾ is Paradise, and ﴿the scorching heat﴾ is Hell. Al-harur (the scorching heat) in the lexical sense is the intensity of heat by day and by night, and al-samum (the scorching wind) specifically by day.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verses 19–21:

﴿And the blind and the seeing are not alike﴾ is an illustration of the disbeliever and the believer. ﴿Nor are the darknesses and the light﴾ is an illustration of disbelief and faith. ﴿Nor the shade and the scorching heat﴾ is an illustration of reward and punishment. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 22:

﴿And the living and the dead are not alike.﴾ This is a parable: the one who has believed is like the living, and the one who has not believed is like the dead. ﴿Indeed, Allah causes to hear whom He wills.﴾ This is an expression for Allah's guidance of whomever He wills. ﴿And you cannot make hear those who are in the graves.﴾ This is an expression for the disbelievers' failure to hear the proofs and admonitions; so He likens them to the dead in their lack of perception. It has also been said: the meaning is that the people of the graves, who are the dead in reality, do not hear, so it is not incumbent upon you to make them hear; rather, you were sent only to the living.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 24:

﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them.﴾ Its meaning is that God has sent to every nation a prophet who establishes the proof against them. If it is said: how is that, when there were gaps (fatarat) and long periods between the prophets? Do you not see that between Jesus and Muhammad, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, there were six hundred years in which no prophet was sent? The answer is that the call of Jesus and of the prophets before him had reached them, so the proof was established against them. If it is said: how is this verse reconciled with His words ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3]? The answer is that no warner contemporary with them had come to them, so this does not conflict with what came before their era. Also, the intended meaning of His words ﴿And there is no nation but that a warner has passed among them﴾ is that the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is not a novelty and should not be denied, because God sent him as He sent those before him. And the intended meaning of His words ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ [al-Sajdah: 3] is that they are in need of warning, since no one who would warn them had preceded; the context of the two statements differs, so there is no contradiction between them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 25–27:

﴿And if they deny you﴾ — this verse is a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ, so that he may take comfort (in the example of earlier messengers). ﴿Nakir﴾ — mentioned in Saba' (the surah of Sheba). ﴿Fruits of diverse colours﴾ — he means yellow, red and other colours. It is said that he means kinds (types), but the first (meaning) is more apparent, because of his mention of white, red and black after that. In both interpretations there is evidence that God Most High is a free and choosing agent, who creates whatever He wills and chooses. It also refutes the naturalists [the materialists (dahriyyun)], for nature does not produce from itself more than one kind. ﴿Judad﴾ — plural of judda, which means the streaks and paths in mountains. ﴿And black ravens﴾ — plural of gharib, which means intensely black. He placed the more emphatic description first, although its proper place was to come later, for the purpose of emphasis, and because this often occurs in the speech of the Arabs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 28:

﴿Thus﴾ is connected to what precedes it, so the pause is complete upon it. The meaning is: among mankind, the beasts and the cattle are those whose colours differ, just like the mountains whose colours differ, and the fruits whose colours differ. All of this is evidence (istidlal) of the power of Allah and His will.

﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge (ʿulamaʾ) fear Allah﴾: it means the scholars of Allah, His attributes and His laws, with a knowledge that necessitates for them fear (khashyah) of His punishment. And in the hadith: "The one among you who knows Allah best is the one who fears Him most." Because when the servant knows Allah, he fears His punishment, and when he does not know Him, he does not fear Him. Therefore the scholars are singled out for fear.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verses 29–31:

﴿Indeed, those who recite the Book of Allah﴾ means: those who read the Qur'an. It was also said: the meaning of ﴿yatlūna﴾ (recite/follow) is: they follow it. The predicate is ﴿yarjūna tijāratan﴾ (they hope for a commerce), or it is omitted. ﴿Lan tabūr﴾ means: it will never fail (lan taksud). By "commerce" is meant seeking reward. ﴿And He will give them their full rewards and increase them from His bounty﴾: tawfiyat al-ujūr (the full payment of wages), which is what the obedient one deserves of reward, and the increase is multiplication beyond that. It was also said: the increase is looking upon the Face of Allah. ﴿Confirming what is before it﴾ has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

﴿Then We caused to inherit the Book those whom We chose﴾. He means the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). Inheritance (al-tawrith) is an expression meaning that Allah gave them the Book after other nations.

﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾. Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ka'b, Aisha, and most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said that these three categories are within the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). So the one who wrongs himself is the disobedient, the foremost is the pious, and the moderate is between them.

Al-Hasan said: the foremost is the one whose good deeds outweigh his bad deeds; the one who wrongs himself is the one whose bad deeds outweigh his good deeds; and the moderate is the one whose good and bad deeds are equal. All of them will enter Paradise. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Our foremost is foremost, our moderate is saved, and our one who wronged himself is forgiven."

It was also said: the one who wrongs himself is the disbeliever, the moderate is the believer who is disobedient, and the foremost is the pious. According to this view, the pronoun in "minhum" (among them) refers to the servants. According to the first view, it refers to "those whom We chose," and this is more likely and more correct because it is found in the hadith, and because of the eminence of those who hold it.

If it is asked: why was the one who wrongs himself mentioned first, the moderate in the middle, and the foremost last? The answer is: He mentioned the one who wrongs himself first out of kindness to him, so that he would not despair, and He mentioned the foremost last so that he would not become conceited. Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned the one who wrongs himself first because of the large number of wrongdoers, and He mentioned the foremost last because of the small number of the foremost.

﴿That is the great bounty﴾, referring to the chosen status.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 35, verse 33:

﴿Gardens of perpetual residence (jannatu ʿadn)﴾ is either a substitution (badal) for "the bounty" (al-fadl), or the predicate of an implied subject, the sense being: "their reward is gardens of perpetual residence," or an implied subject, the sense being: "for them are gardens of perpetual residence." ﴿They will enter them﴾: the pronoun of the subject refers to the wrongdoer (al-zalim), the moderate (al-muqtasid), and the foremost in good deeds (al-sabiq), on the view that the verse concerns this Ummah. As for the view that the wrongdoer is the disbeliever, the pronoun refers only to the moderate and the foremost. Al-Zamakhshari said that it refers only to the foremost, and that is according to the view of the Mu'tazilah on the threat (al-wa'id). ﴿Bracelets (asawir)﴾: this was mentioned in Surah al-Hajj [22:23].

﴿Who has removed from us the grief﴾. It was said that it is the torment of the Fire. It was also said that it is the terrors of the Resurrection. And it was said that it is the worries of this world. The correct view is that the meaning is general, encompassing all of that.

﴿The abode of permanence﴾ is Paradise. Al-maqama is al-iqama (residence), and the place. Paradise is called "the abode of permanence" because its people stand (yaqumuna) in it and do not leave it. ﴿Fatigue﴾: al-nasab is weariness of the body, and al-lughub is weariness of the soul, which is the one that follows from weariness of the body.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 37:

﴿يَصْطَرِخُونَ﴾ (yaṣṭarikhūna) is a reflexive form (yaftaʿilūna) derived from ṣurākh (crying out), meaning they cry out for help, saying: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out﴾ And in their saying: ﴿other than what we used to do﴾ is an acknowledgment of the evil of their deeds and a regret for them.

﴿Did We not grant you a life long enough for whoever would remember to remember?﴾ The verse is a rebuke to them and the establishment of proof against them. It was said: the period of admonition is sixty years; it was said: forty; and it was said: maturity (al-bulugh). The first is more preponderant, due to the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever Allah grants a life of sixty years has left him no excuse regarding his lifespan."

﴿And the warner came to you﴾ means the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: it means white hair (al-shayb), because it is a warner of death. The first is more apparent.

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ That is, of what the breasts conceal and believe. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Here *ذات* (dhāt) is the feminine of *ذو* (dhū), in the sense of *صاحب* (ṣāḥib, possessor), because the concealed things accompany the breasts."
﴿Khalā'if﴾ (successors), which was mentioned in al-An'am. ﴿Maqtan﴾ (hatred). Al-maqt is a person's contempt for someone and his hatred of him because of that person's faults or sins.

**Say: Have you considered your partners...** [This verse is] an argument against the polytheists and a refutation of their position. **"Or do they have a share (shirk), that is, a portion, in it"** ... **"upon clear evidence"** Nafi' read *bayyinat* (plural, "clear proofs"), meaning upon a matter that is evident. The pronoun in *ātaynāhum* (We have given them) may refer to the idols or to the polytheists, and the latter is more apparent in meaning. The former, however, fits better with the pronouns that precede it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 41:

﴿That they should not cease﴾ is in the position of an object of purpose, its sense being "out of aversion that they should cease," or it is a direct object, since "yumsik" (holds back) carries the meaning of "yamna'" (prevents). ﴿And if they should cease﴾ means: even supposing their cessation were to occur, no one would hold them back. It was also said: He intends their cessation on the Day of Resurrection, at the folding up of the heavens, the changing of the earth, and the blowing away of the mountains. ﴿After Him﴾ means: after His withholding of them ceases.

"And they swore by God" — the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, because they said: "May God curse the Jews and the Christians; messengers came to them and they denied them. By God, if a messenger comes to us, we will surely be better guided than them." "One of the nations" — meaning the Jews and the Christians. "But when a warner came to them" — meaning Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 35, verse 43:

﴿ٱسْتِكْبَاراً﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿نفوراً﴾, or an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi): ﴿arrogance﴾. ﴿وَمَكْرَ ٱلسَّيِّىءِ﴾ is an example of an adjective being added to the noun it describes (idafat al-sifah ila al-mawsuf), like your saying "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque) and "janib al-gharbi" (the western side). The original form would be "al-makr al-sayyi'" (the evil scheming). ﴿وَلاَ يَحِيقُ ٱلْمَكْرُ ٱلسَّيِّىءُ إِلاَّ بِأَهْلِهِ﴾ means: the harm of evil scheming does not encompass anyone except the one who schemed and plotted it. Ka'b said to Ibn 'Abbas: "In the Torah, whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it." Ibn 'Abbas said: "I find this in the Book of Allah: ﴿And evil scheming does not encompass anyone except its own people﴾." ﴿فَهَلْ يَنظُرُونَ إِلاَّ سُنَّتَ ٱلأَوَّلِينَ﴾ means: do they await anything except the custom of the earlier nations, in Allah's seizing them and destroying them for [rejecting] the messengers?

Qur'anic quotation: "Nor is it that Allah could be frustrated by anything..." — I need to translate plainly inside the markers.

Translation:

﴿Nor was Allah ever such that anything could render Him powerless﴾, meaning: nothing escapes Him, and nothing is difficult for Him.

Translation:

﴿He has not left upon its back any creature﴾: the pronoun refers to the earth, and "creature" (dābba) is general, covering everything that crawls upon it. It is also said that He meant specifically the children of Adam. ﴿Until an appointed term﴾: that is, the Day of Resurrection. The rest of the verse is a promise and a warning.
